extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and applicants (patent attorneys, applicants), USPTO examiners and policy makers
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether to appeal USPTO rejections to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB) using empirical reversal statistics and strategic considerations (including c-term PTA, pendency, and costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use individual-rejection reversal rates rather than overall decision labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-rejection reversal rates (e.g., for 35 U.S.C. § 112 Written Description, Enablement, Indefiniteness; § 102; § 103; § 101) give a more accurate prediction of an applicant's chances on a particular issue than the USPTO's case-level labels (Affirmed / Affirmed-in-Part / Reversed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper provides sampled reversal rates (95% confidence, 5% CI) for individual rejection types (e.g., Enablement ~60.9% reversed, Written Description ~50.8% reversed, Indefiniteness ~49.5% reversed, §102(a) ~50.5% reversed, §103(a) ~40.5% reversed, §101 ~24.7% reversed). These per-rejection statistics are more useful to applicants deciding whether to appeal than the USPTO’s aggregated case-label percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand PTAB decision labeling rules and their bias
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision is labeled 'Reversed' only if every rejection on appeal is reversed; any affirmed rejection prevents that label. 'Affirmed' vs 'Affirmed-in-Part' depends on whether any claim is left free of rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this labeling, the USPTO statistics under-report reversals and over-report affirmances for individual rejections. Applicants should not rely on the single case-level label for inferences about treatment of specific rejection types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count on c-term PTA eligibility if any rejection is reversed
rubrics_metrics.description: An application is eligible for c-term Patent Term Adjustment (extra patent term equal to appeal pendency) if any rejection is reversed by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because PTA eligibility is triggered by any reversed rejection, applicants valuing PTA should consider bringing multiple rejections to appeal. The paper notes that for 2016 at least 41.5% of cases were eligible for c-term PTA and that the true rate is likely higher because of unlabeled partial reversals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reversal-to-affirmance ratio as the key indicator of Board treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The ratio of reversals to affirmances for a given rejection type is the best statistical indicator of how the Board treats that issue and of an applicant’s likelihood of success on that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmed-in-Part cases should be assumed to maintain the same reversal:affirm ratio for the given rejection type. The paper recommends using the ratio rather than raw percentages that omit the meaning of Affirmed-in-Part splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider how often a rejection type is appealed (contentiousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative frequency that a rejection type is taken to the Board indicates contentiousness between Examiners and Applicants over that issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study found §103 (obviousness) is by far the most appealed (~11,000), §102 next (~2,000), §101 and §112 indefiniteness ~1,000, §112 written description ~700, and §112 enablement ~250. High appeal frequency paired with reversal data informs strategy and signals areas needing Office guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for three-examiner panel pre-decision withdrawals
rubrics_metrics.description: After an appeal brief is filed, a three-Examiner panel preliminarily reviews the case and may withdraw rejections or the entire appeal (i.e., reopen prosecution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical/firm experience suggests withdrawal rates may be between 25% and 50%. Including expected panel withdrawals can materially increase an applicant’s practical chances of success (e.g., a 20% withdrawal rate on single-issue obviousness cases can push ‘effective’ success over 50%). Applicants should factor panel withdrawal probabilities into appeal decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic tradeoff: minimize rejections for full reversal vs maximize for PTA
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant's objective is a full reversal/notice of allowance, take as few rejections to appeal as possible; if the objective is c-term PTA, take as many rejections as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More rejections give the Board more opportunities to affirm at least one (reducing chance of full reversal) but also more opportunities to reverse at least one (increasing chance of PTA). The paper’s example: with four different rejections, full-reversal chances are low but chance of at least one reversal (and thus PTA) is very high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust expectations and tactics by statutory rejection type
rubrics_metrics.description: Each statute has different observed reversal behavior: enablement (~60.9% reversed) is applicant-friendly; written description, anticipation, and indefiniteness are often reversed (~50%); obviousness (~40% reversed) and subject-matter eligibility (§101, ~24.7% reversed) are harder to overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should weigh these empirical rates when deciding to appeal, prioritize arguments accordingly (e.g., give special attention to secondary independent claims and dependent claims in obviousness cases), and be cautious about pursuing §101 appeals absent strong grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 50% reversal rate as a heuristic benchmark for calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: In an ideal, well-calibrated system, reversal rates would be about 50% — indicating balanced assessment by Examiners and applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reversal rate >50% suggests Examiners are over-rejecting that issue; <50% suggests applicants are overestimating their positions or the law is unsettled. This heuristic informs whether procedural or substantive adjustments are needed from Examiners or applicants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of 'Affirmed-in-Part' labelling
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Affirmed-in-Part' means the Board considered multiple rejections of the same type and reversed at least one and affirmed at least one, but it conceals how many or which rejections of that type were reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 'Affirmed-in-Part' mixes reversed and affirmed instances of the same rejection type, analysts should disaggregate per-rejection outcomes (or assume maintenance of the reversal:affirm ratio) when estimating chances per issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor in appeal pendency and government fees when deciding to appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal pendency averages about 18–24 months and government fees for appeal are nearly $3,000 for large entities, so appeals carry significant time and monetary costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should weigh expected benefit (likelihood of reversal, PTA value, chance of next-action allowance) against these costs and delays when deciding whether to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ adequate empirical sampling methodology when estimating rates
rubrics_metrics.description: When producing per-rejection statistics, use sufficiently large random samples with stated confidence level and interval and spread samples across the studied time period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study sampled each rejection type to achieve a 95% confidence level and a 5% confidence interval and distributed samples evenly across the two-year period (Oct 2015–Oct 2017). It references a sample-size calculator to justify sample sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO should report per-rejection disposition statistics and consider relabeling
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board could improve public usefulness of statistics by reporting outcomes for each individual rejection and/or labeling any decision with at least one reversed rejection as 'Reversed'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better reporting would allow applicants and the Office to predict success rates, modify behavior, and improve examination quality. The paper argues such changes would be low-cost and reduce unnecessary appeals and pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and provide guidance where high appeal rates and low reversal rates coincide (e.g., §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: High appeal frequency combined with low reversal rates indicates confusion or disagreement in the applicant community and may warrant additional guidance from the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper highlights §101 as an example (low reversal rate, relatively high appeal rate) and notes the USPTO's subject-matter eligibility guidance (since 2014) but recommends further clarity and consistency; legislative or higher-court change may also affect these outcomes.
